deep_dive.title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
deep_dive.abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

deep_dive.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence with Learning Style Models: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
deep_dive.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for transforming learning. This review examines how Generative AI can be integrated with established learning style models (VARK, Kolb, Felder-Silverman, and Honey & Mumford) to support student engagement in large online classes. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (2015 to 2026) and included 41 studies that met the eligibility criteria. The review maps Generative AI capabilities to learning style preferences, synthesizes existing implementations, highlights benefits and challenges, and proposes pathways for future research and practice. Despite ongoing debates regarding the empirical validity of learning styles, Generative AI enables flexible, multimodal, and real-time adaptation. This study offers practical insights for educators and developers seeking to build more effective, learner centered learning systems

deep_dive.title: AI-generated support, worked examples, and script-based learning in undergraduate physics: A comparative study
deep_dive.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support students during learning and problem solving, but its instructional value depends on how it is embedded in established learning approaches. Worked examples guide learners through the steps and reasoning of a solution; conversational AI may extend them by responding to individual questions. To isolate this added value, we compared a chatbot-delivered intelligent worked example with a matched static worked example and a lecture script. Nine recitation groups in an undergraduate electrodynamics course were cluster-randomized to the three conditions, and 86 students worked individually on a Gauss's law problem. Concept-test accuracy and self-efficacy increased significantly in all conditions, but changes did not differ significantly between groups (p=.07 for concept-test accuracy and p=.38 for self-efficacy). Four weeks later, in a reduced sample with selective participation and pre-existing group differences, students in the static worked-example condition scored higher than those in the script condition (p=.004, d=1.22), whereas the two worked-example conditions did not differ significantly. Usability, but not perceived educational value, was higher for the intelligent worked example than for the script (p=.011, d=0.88). In a subsequent homework assignment on Ampere's law with free choice of learning material (N=46), 62-71% of students in each condition reported using only the static worked example, at most 8% used exclusively the intelligent one, and 15-31% used neither. Thus, conversational delivery showed no clear additional learning benefit under the present conditions. More broadly, a learning format that is rated favorably need not be the one students voluntarily adopt.

deep_dive.title: Validating LLM-Based Essay Scorers: A Comparative Analysis in Critical Online Reasoning in Medical Education
deep_dive.abstract: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.

deep_dive.title: Share your Screen and Talk to Gemini: How Young Learners Interact with Multimodal GenAI While Solving Scratch Tasks
deep_dive.abstract: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging. Verbal interactions based on screen sharing or camera data may be an interesting alternative for supporting learners. We therefore explore the quality, use, and perceptions of fifth- and sixth-graders' verbal interactions with a GenAI tutor. The goal is to investigate the quality and use of the multimodal GenAI tutor in the given context. First of all, a pilot study of eight tasks conducted without students helped inform the process of the tutor's classroom evaluation. The classroom study was realized after fifth- and sixth-graders had participated in six Scratch classroom lessons. Then 23 students were introduced to the tutor, worked on the eight tasks with the GenAI tutor, and completed a questionnaire. The analysis of the pilot and classroom study shows that the tutor's responses were intelligible and actionable, and no single turn revealed a complete solution. However, the tutor missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns, compared to 15.7% in the pilot study. Children's voice prompts were brief and mostly responded to the tutor. Although a video had explained that responses could be incorrect, 39.1% of the children trusted the tutor's answers to always be correct. These findings have implications for educators and learners using multimodal GenAI tutors, as they need to be aware that an intelligible and human-like voice does not ensure correct support. For developers, our results suggest that screen sharing alone does not ensure responses that match the program state.

deep_dive.title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
deep_dive.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

quick_skim.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
quick_skim.abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

quick_skim.title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
quick_skim.abstract: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

quick_skim.title: Open Response Explorer: a Structured Collaborative Writing System for Peer-Informed Open-Response Assignments
quick_skim.abstract: Peer-informed open-response assignments (where students view, connect, and learn from peer contributions) hold the potential to foster collaborative knowledge building, yet the unstructured nature of free-form prose prevents students from effectively comparing and making sense of peers' work. We present Open Response Explorer, an interface that recenters open responses on structured idea units through purpose-based writing and peer response exploration, augmented by common-role text segment highlighting for easy comparison. A within-subjects lab study (N=12) validated the usefulness and usability of the system, demonstrating how it shaped the open-response drafting and peer exploration practices. We discuss implications for purpose-centered authoring and exploration that transform free-form prose into structured, comparable, and collectively navigable knowledge artifacts.

quick_skim.title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
quick_skim.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.

quick_skim.title: AI as Anchor: How Interview Sequencing Relates to the Appropriation of Synthetic Stakeholder Voices in Design Education
quick_skim.abstract: Designers increasingly use large language models to simulate stakeholder conversations. Yet it remains unclear how AI-Simulated Stakeholders (AIS) are taken up when used alongside human stakeholder engagement. We report a field study in a single-institution, single-semester design course in which 8 teams (N=21) constructed, evaluated, and peer-reviewed an initial AIS. Then, the teams interviewed both AIS and human stakeholders in two sequences: AIS-first or human-first. Drawing on interview transcripts, design artifacts, course-embedded reflections, and post-course qualitative sessions, we examine exploratory patterns associated with these sequencing conditions. We find that students did not describe AIS as a neutral addition to the process. Instead, the order in which AIS and human stakeholders were formally interviewed was associated with different ways of interpreting and using information from the two sources. When the AIS interview came first, it provided a broad but often general frame that students later reconsidered through human interviews. When the AIS interview followed human engagement, AIS was more often used to revisit and validate insights already grounded in lived experience. Students described AIS as an "anchor," but its reported role varied with its position in the formal interview sequence. In the final designs, a larger proportion of prominent human-stakeholder-derived concerns than AIS-derived concerns had corresponding design elements. We contribute: characterization of AIS as a reference point whose reported role varies with its position in the formal interview sequence; exploratory empirical evidence that the implemented interview-order conditions were associated with distinct patterns of interpreting and using stakeholder input; and implications for integrating AIS into design workflows in ways that preserve direct engagement with human stakeholders

quick_skim.title: COSIMA Cookbook: a community-driven resource for ocean and sea-ice modelling science
quick_skim.abstract: The COSIMA Cookbook is an open educational resource for analysing ocean and sea-ice model output in Jupyter notebooks. It has been developed by the Consortium for Ocean--Sea Ice Modelling in Australia (COSIMA) as a community resource for researchers, students, and practitioners working with large gridded datasets, especially output from the ACCESS ocean--sea ice model configurations. The Cookbook is organised around a gastronomy theme: ``Cooking Tutorials'' teach generic, transferable techniques for handling model output, while "Easy Recipes", "Advanced Recipes" and "Regional Specialties" are self-contained notebooks that show how to perform concrete diagnostics and analyses. Along the way, the notebooks demonstrate open-source tools for the scientific analysis of large data, including Intake catalogues, Xarray, Dask, xgcm, xESMF, eofs, Parcels, matplotlib and Cartopy. The Cookbook addresses the steep entry cost of analysing climate model output: it packages expert, often tacit, knowledge into complete, well-documented and reusable workflows, in the same medium in which researchers actually work. It is developed openly on GitHub, is published as a documentation website, and is continuously reviewed and extended by its community through pull requests and regular hackathons. The easy access to data and analysis it provides has contributed to the international adoption of ACCESS ocean and sea-ice model configurations, and has facilitated well over 100 peer-reviewed papers and more than 20 PhD projects.

quick_skim.title: Explain Your Code: AI-Based Examination at Class Scale
quick_skim.abstract: Generative AI has weakened the link between working code and a student's understanding of it. Oral examination, the traditional test of that understanding, does not scale to large courses. We report the full-course deployment of a three-agent AI system that examines students on their own code. The first, the examiner, asks three questions anchored to specific lines of the submission, adapting difficulty to each answer, in a 16-minute text dialogue. The other two grade: a code reviewer that never sees the examination and a grader without direct access to the code. Authorship is assessed separately and is advisory. The system examined 247 students in an operating systems course (three exercises, 546 sittings, two examination languages). The grader's oral score was uncorrelated with the same submission's code quality score (Spearman rho = -0.073, 95% CI [-0.205, 0.063], n = 216) yet tracked degree grade point average (rho = 0.419, [0.294, 0.523], n = 214), while automated test scores sat at the ceiling. The mean of a student's two oral scores correlated with grade point average at 0.468 ([0.353, 0.568], n = 210), within the range of grades in three single-semester courses built on programming assignments. Model spend averaged at most $1.37 per sitting. In surveys, students began skeptical of the AI examination and rated it more favorably after sitting it twice. These results indicate that examining students on their own code is feasible at class scale, and that its score relates to academic standing where the code quality score does not.

quick_skim.title: WIP: Exploring Student-Created AI Agents and Instructional Videos to Foster Engagement in Computing Education
quick_skim.abstract: This work-in-progress (WIP) research-to-practice study examines the use of student-created artifacts to promote active learning in a large undergraduate Software Design and Engineering (SWE) course. Active learning strategies have been shown to significantly enhance student engagement, comprehension, and motivation, particularly in computing education. In this work, we explore the use of student-created artifacts to foster student engagement in higher-level Computer Science (CS) courses. Specifically, we examine the experiences of undergraduate and graduate CS students who participated in the creation of two types of artifacts: instructional video tutorials and conversational AI agents. The goal being to understand how designing these artifacts could support students in applying and learning course content. Students raised valuable insights regarding both experiences. Concerning the creation of instructional videos, they appreciated the interactivity brought through multimedia to their learning experiences, although some found the strategy to be time-consuming. Similarly, when designing conversational AI agents, students enjoyed the novelty and practical application of the task, while some encountered challenges related to the complexity of tools such as \textit{Google Dialogflow ES}. We report on the potential of student-created artifacts to foster deeper engagement with course material, encouraging both creativity and critical thinking in computing education.

quick_skim.title: Lecture Board Readability as an AI-Measurable Predictor of Perceived Teaching Clarity
quick_skim.abstract: Lecture boards remain central to university teaching in physics and mathematics, yet the visual quality of what instructors write has rarely been measured systematically. We examined whether a vision-language model can score board writing in a way that relates to how students perceive instruction. We analysed 2,645 board images from 56 university physics and applied mathematics courses taught by 18 lecturers, scoring each image 50 times with Claude 3.5 Sonnet on readability, organization and visual elements. Course-level readability was associated with student-rated clarity ($r$ = .43) and organization ($r$ = .46), and remained the only significant predictor of the overall survey score after controlling for class size, mean course grade and study year. These associations were robust to clustering by lecturer and remained stable when only one or two images per lecture were used. In a subsample of 100 images rated by four human raters, agreement between AI and human scores was comparable to agreement among the raters themselves for visual elements, lower for readability and weakest for organization. Student evaluations served as a benchmark of perceived clarity rather than of teaching quality as a whole. Automated analysis of board images may offer a low-cost, scalable source of formative feedback in STEM teaching.

quick_skim.title: Miscalibrated AI improves human calibration: An alignment problem for AI-assisted Decision education
quick_skim.abstract: Using artificial intelligence (AI) well requires probabilistic thinking, and central to it is calibration: expressing certainty that matches one's actual accuracy. Calibration is a decision skill, but a notoriously difficult one to teach. Because AI systems typically generate a probability alongside every prediction, observing these probabilities may help humans learn to provide better calibrated judgments. This is one form of what we call AI-assisted decision education -- using AI to teach the judgment skills that decision-making requires -- of which learning by observation, as here, is among the simplest forms. In a preregistered experiment, novice participants (N = 300) judged the probability that images of white blood cells were cancerous, before and after exposure to a highly accurate (94%) convolutional neural network. A single model was shown in three ways, holding accuracy fixed while varying the certainty it expressed: its original probabilities, which were conservative and poorly calibrated for the model's accuracy; a recalibrated version, well calibrated for the model and correspondingly certain; or categorical predictions carrying no probability information. When later tested without the AI, only the original, conservative display improved participants' calibration. It did so by reducing over-extremity, without a condition-specific improvement in discrimination. Notably, the display that taught best was the one miscalibrated for the model. AI-assisted decision education therefore faces an alignment problem: the signal that best describes a model, need not be the signal that best supports the learner.
quick_skim.llm_evidence_en: AI-assisted decision education using AI probabilities to teach calibration

quick_skim.llm_tldr_cn: 概率校准是决策中的关键技能却难以教授，本文提出AI辅助决策教育，利用AI在每次预测时给出的概率让学习者通过观察来学习校准。研究开展预注册实验，300名新手完成图像概率判断任务，结果显示即便AI自身校准失准，其输出仍能改善人类的校准水平。该工作揭示了AI教学工具面临的对齐问题，并为以AI培养判断技能提供了实证依据。

quick_skim.title: Standard-Anchored Delegation in Teachers' Use of Generative AI
quick_skim.abstract: Teachers who use generative AI must decide which parts of their work to hand over, while they remain accountable for what reaches students. We studied these decisions in Punjab, Pakistan, through a qualitatively driven mixed-methods study. We interviewed 13 teachers from government, private, NGO and vocational institutions, four administrators and one student, and coded each teacher's position on twelve educational tasks. Nine teachers accepted AI drafts or substantial assistance with lesson planning, but none accepted AI-drafted learning objectives, and eleven did not use AI to encourage or emotionally support students. Teachers who would accept AI marking required that the model be given a rubric or marking criteria. Building on assessment research and HCI work on verifiability, we call this pattern standard-anchored delegation: teachers handed a component of a task to AI when a standard outside the model, such as a textbook or rubric, defined a correct output and the teacher could apply that standard to the result. Having a standard was not always enough. Several government-school teachers did not use AI to mark quizzes even though the quizzes had answer keys, because they expected students to look for evidence of the teacher's effort. Checking AI output required subject knowledge and time, and private schools gave teachers more support for this than government schools did. Participants also read disclosure of AI use as a statement about whether the teacher had reviewed the work. We propose that teacher-facing AI tools ask for the relevant standard before generating and show each output beside it, and that schools account for the time that checking takes.

quick_skim.llm_tldr_en: A mixed-methods study in Punjab interviews teachers and administrators to examine which educational tasks they delegate to generative AI, finding selective acceptance of AI drafts but firm boundaries on objectives and emotional support.
quick_skim.llm_tldr_cn: 针对教师使用生成式AI时如何划定委托边界、又须对学生负责的问题，该文在巴基斯坦旁遮普省开展质性主导的混合方法研究，访谈13名教师、4名管理者与1名学生，并对12项教学任务逐项编码。结果显示九名教师接受AI起草或辅助备课，但无人接受AI拟定学习目标，多数不用于情感支持，接受AI评分者要求提供评分标准。研究为教学场景中的人机分工与责任设计提供依据。
